title: Creole and Cajun
intro: The roux, the trinity and the great pots of south Louisiana, and where the city's Creole cooking parts from the Cajun cooking of the country. Gumbo, étouffée and jambalaya are the lessons.

entries.title: The holy trinity and the mirepoix
entries.summary: Onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and softened together at the start of a Creole or Cajun dish. It is south Louisiana's answer to the French mirepoix, with green pepper standing where the carrot would be.
entries.guest: The holy trinity is onion, celery and green pepper cooked together. It is the base of our gumbo, the turtle soup and the Creole sauce on the shrimp and grits.

paras: The holy trinity is the aromatic base of south Louisiana cooking: onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and cooked together in fat until soft. It plays the part that mirepoix plays in a French kitchen, and the difference is the point. Where mirepoix takes carrot, the trinity takes green pepper, which gives a sharper, greener savour and none of the carrot's sugar.

It is shared by both of Louisiana's great cooking traditions. Creole cooking, the city cooking of New Orleans, puts it under tomato, butter and stock; Cajun cooking, from the prairies and bayous to the west, puts it into dark roux, game and smoked meat.

Mirepoix itself is classically two parts onion to one part each of carrot and celery, by weight, cut small for a sauce and large for a long-simmered stock. A white mirepoix leaves out the carrot, often taking leek in its place, so that a pale stock or sauce stays pale. A matignon is a mirepoix cooked gently in butter, often with ham, and left in the dish to be eaten rather than strained out.

The vegetables are old in Louisiana kitchens; the name is newer. It nods to the Catholic faith of south Louisiana and is widely said to have been popularised, and perhaps coined, by the chef Paul Prudhomme in the 1980s. Garlic is added so often that some cooks call it the pope.

Ratios vary by cook. Many use equal parts of all three; others follow the mirepoix habit of two parts onion to one part each of celery and pepper, which gives a rounder, sweeter base. For a pot of gumbo for eight, about 300 g of diced onion to 150 g each of celery and green pepper is a sound start.

Cut the three to the same small dice so they soften together. In a gumbo or an étouffée the trinity goes straight into the hot roux, which stops the roux from darkening any further and cooks the vegetables in its heat; stir hard, because the pot will hiss and steam. Elsewhere it is sweated in butter or oil over moderate heat until soft and translucent, ten minutes or so, before the garlic and then the liquid go in.

At Brennan's the trinity is in the Seafood Gumbo, the Turtle Soup, the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing. It is why those dishes taste of Louisiana before a single spice goes in, and a guest who asks what makes a gumbo Creole can be told to start there.

ratios.label: Equal parts
ratios.value: Onion, celery and green pepper, one part each

ratios.label: The mirepoix habit
ratios.value: Two parts onion to one part each of celery and green pepper

faults.fault: Hard pieces in the finished pot
faults.cause: Uneven dice, so some pieces cooked through and others did not.
faults.fix: Cut all three to the same small dice before the roux is ready.

faults.fault: Scorched roux when the vegetables go in
faults.cause: The trinity was not ready and the roux kept darkening.
faults.fix: Have the diced trinity beside the stove before the roux starts, and add it the moment the colour is right.

faults.cause: Too much onion, or the vegetables browned instead of softening.
faults.fix: Keep to the chosen ratio and soften over moderate heat.

brennans.how: The trinity goes into the roux at the start of the Seafood Gumbo, under the shrimp, crab, oysters and andouille.
It builds the base of the Turtle Soup before the stock and the turtle meat go in, long before the finishing Sherry.
It starts the Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits, a tomato sauce carrying tasso, the spiced smoked pork.
The trinity seasons the South Louisiana Rice Dressing, the rice side served at dinner.

cards.front: Which three vegetables make the holy trinity?
cards.back: Onion, celery and green bell pepper, diced and softened together at the start of a Creole or Cajun dish.

cards.front: How does the trinity differ from a French mirepoix?
cards.back: Mirepoix uses carrot; the trinity puts green bell pepper in its place, for a sharper, less sugary base.

cards.front: Where does the name holy trinity come from?
cards.back: It nods to the Catholic faith of south Louisiana; the chef Paul Prudhomme is widely said to have popularised it in the 1980s.

cards.front: What do some cooks call the garlic added to the trinity?
cards.back: The pope, a joke on the name, because garlic joins the three so often.

cards.front: What ratios do cooks use for the trinity?
cards.back: Equal parts of all three, or the mirepoix habit of two parts onion to one part each of celery and green pepper.

cards.front: What happens when the trinity goes into a hot dark roux?
cards.back: It stops the roux darkening further and cooks in the roux's heat; the pot hisses and steams, so stir hard.

cards.front: Why cut the three vegetables to the same size?
cards.back: So they soften at the same rate and melt into the dish together instead of leaving hard pieces.

cards.front: What is the classic ratio of a French mirepoix?
cards.back: Two parts onion to one part each of carrot and celery, by weight, cut small for a sauce and large for a stock.

cards.front: What is a white mirepoix, and why use one?
cards.back: A mirepoix without carrot, often with leek in its place, so that a pale stock or sauce keeps its colour.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes start with the trinity?
cards.back: The Seafood Gumbo, the Turtle Soup, the Creole sauce on the Shrimp & Grits and the South Louisiana Rice Dressing.

questions.q: Which vegetables make up the holy trinity of Louisiana cooking?
questions.answer: Onion, celery and green bell pepper
questions.why: Onion, celery and green pepper are the three; onion, carrot and celery is the French mirepoix that the trinity adapts.

questions.q: Which vegetable of the French mirepoix does the trinity replace with green pepper?
questions.why: Mirepoix is onion, carrot and celery; Louisiana kept the onion and celery and put green bell pepper where the carrot was.

questions.q: In kitchen slang, what is the pope added to the trinity?
questions.why: Garlic joins the three so often that cooks joke it is the pope, keeping the religious name going.

questions.q: What does adding the trinity to a hot dark roux do?
questions.answer: Stops the roux darkening and cooks the vegetables
distractors: Thickens the roux into a stiff paste
Turns the roux black at once
questions.why: The cool, wet vegetables drop the roux's temperature and halt its colour, while its heat softens them; that is why they go in at the chosen colour.

questions.q: Who is widely said to have popularised the name holy trinity?
questions.why: Prudhomme, the Louisiana chef, is widely credited with spreading the phrase in the 1980s; the three vegetables themselves are far older.

questions.q: Which Brennan's dish has the trinity in its base?
questions.why: The trinity goes into the gumbo's roux; Bananas Foster, the Sardou and the Lemon Tart are built on other foundations.

questions.q: What is the classic proportion of a French mirepoix, by weight?
questions.answer: Two parts onion to one each of carrot and celery
distractors: Equal parts onion, carrot and celery
Two parts carrot to one each of onion and celery
Two parts celery to one each of onion and carrot
questions.why: Classical mirepoix leans on onion, two parts to one each of carrot and celery; the trinity keeps the onion and swaps the carrot for green pepper.

questions.q: Why are the three vegetables cut to the same small dice?
questions.answer: So they soften at the same rate
distractors: So they brown as darkly as possible
So they can be lifted out later
So the pot needs less stirring
questions.why: Even pieces cook through together and melt into the dish; uneven ones leave some hard while others collapse.

steps.title: Build a gumbo
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a seafood gumbo in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cook flour in oil, stirring constantly, to a dark brown roux
Add the holy trinity to stop the roux and soften the vegetables
Stir in garlic and sliced andouille
Whisk in hot stock a ladle at a time and bring it to a simmer
Simmer for about an hour, skimming the fat and seasoning as it goes
Add the shrimp, crab and oysters at the end and cook them just through
Finish with green onion and parsley and serve over rice
steps.distractor: Thicken it at the end with a slurry of cornflour and cream
steps.why: The roux is cooked to colour first, the trinity halts it, and the stock goes in before the long simmer; the seafood comes last so it does not toughen.
